description: We are an Edmonton Based team that is interested in cybersecurity, AI, and machine learning.
summary: Freefall Fire Atlas is a web dashboard that turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion repository into fire-safety insight for crews heading to the Moon and Mars. It ranks the 24 combustion investigations in PSI by how directly they inform fire safety in a chosen habitat, and it maps 2,282 rows of run data against the cabin atmospheres NASA plans to fly. The main finding: the challenge brief expects lunar habitat air at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, yet no solid-material row in PSI goes above 22.7% oxygen, and all 20 logged runs inside that region are gas flames. A gap matrix and five ranked gaps show which fire questions still lack open data, and which flown or planned experiments could close them. This matters because more oxygen at lower pressure makes cabin materials easier to ignite, and material tests are still run in normal gravity on Earth.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Freefall Fire Atlas is a single-file website with six tabs.

  • Overview: a plain-language key finding, with counts computed live from the embedded data.
  • Map: every PSI run with a recorded chamber oxygen level, plotted against pressure and colored by fuel type (solid materials, liquid droplets, gas flames). Five target cabin atmospheres are drawn as boxes: ISS cabin, Orion and transit vehicle, lunar habitat and rover, Mars transit habitat, and Mars surface habitat. NASA results that are not in PSI (Saffire IV–VI, SoFIE-GEL, LUCI) appear as a separate labeled layer.
  • Gaps: a matrix of the five environments against six fire hazards (ignition and flammability limits, flame spread over solids, extinction and suppression, smoke and detection, smoldering, partial gravity). Each cell counts the PSI runs near that atmosphere, and clicking a cell lists them. Five ranked gaps follow, each with what is missing, why it matters, the nearest data and what experiment could close it, plus a briefing per environment.
  • Ranking: the 24 PSI investigations scored on seven criteria for a chosen habitat, with adjustable weights, full record text, DOIs and side-by-side compare.
  • Context: findings from the ISS combustion program, Earth applications and the fires that set the agenda.
  • About: sources, method, scoring rules, limits, and the AI and human contributions.

What the data shows: 987 logged PSI runs have both oxygen and pressure. 20 fall inside the brief's lunar region (30% O2 or more at 10.2 psi or less), and all 20 are ACME CFI-G gas flames. PSI holds 261 solid-material rows with an oxygen level; none is above 22.7% O2, and every one with a recorded pressure sits at 0.97–1.01 atm. The only solid-material flight burns near the NASA lunar target (30–34% O2 at 8.2–10.2 psia) are 3 Saffire-VI tests, which are in NASA papers but not in PSI. PSI has no runs at lunar or Martian gravity.

How does it work?

  • Data: all 24 PSI combustion investigation records and their experiment tables were pulled from the PSI repository on 14 November 2026 and merged into one table of 2,282 rows with common units (oxygen in percent, pressure in atm, flow in cm/s).
  • Counting: the site embeds every row and counts in the browser, so no number in the map or gap sections is typed in. Inverse-flame rows are excluded from chamber-oxygen counts, FLEX-2 test-matrix rows are never counted as runs, and rows with missing pressure or oxygen are shown separately.
  • Matching: a run is “near” an environment when its oxygen is within ±3 percentage points and its pressure within ±20% of the environment's range.
  • Scoring: relevance score = weighted average of seven 0–5 ratings, scaled to 100. Gap risk = data gap × hazard weight × isolation from Earth, ranked on environments whose values are all cited. The rules and weights are shown on the site.
  • Build: one self-contained HTML file with plain JavaScript and hand-drawn SVG charts, no chart library. It works offline, supports light and dark mode, and gives every chart a table view.

What benefits does it have?

  • It makes a large, hard-to-compare repository readable: one map, one matrix and one ranked list.
  • It separates what PSI covers from what only exists in NASA papers, and labels each source.
  • Every count can be traced to its runs, and every investigation links to its PSI page and DOI.
  • It shows where new microgravity or partial-gravity burns, or new PSI data releases, would add the most.
  • The same data is relevant on Earth, for smoke detection and for fire behavior in oxygen-enriched settings.

What do you hope to achieve?

We hope the Atlas helps students, researchers and engineers see quickly which fire questions NASA's open data already answers for Moon and Mars cabins, and which it does not. We also hope it encourages adding the Saffire IV–VI, SoFIE, LUCI and FM2 results to PSI, and the missing pressure and oxygen columns to existing tables, so the gaps can be re-counted as data arrives.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the site; Python for data extraction, cleaning and checks.
  • AI: Claude from Anthropic (Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2).
  • Data sources: NASA PSI repository and the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. The site runs in any modern web browser.
